I've switched to buying pre-peeled garlic and then freezing it. When I need it, I take out a few cloves, let them thaw for just a couple minutes, and microplane it. It'll be firm enough from being still slightly frozen to be easy to microplane, and the end result is like a puree. The biggest problem with freezing garlic is that the cellular structure breaks down and it becomes less than ideal for mincing or chopping. However, if anything this makes it perfect for microplaning - much easier than trying to do that from fresh. And the garlic can last substantially longer in a ziploc in the freezer than sitting out.

I make my own garlic paste in a food processor — put a heap of peeled garlic cloves into the processor, then you need to add some liquid to prevent the chopped stuff just sticking to the sides of the bowl. I use vodka. It's tasteless and serves as a preservative. You can keep the paste in the fridge in a glass jar for at least a month — my supply never lasts that long, since I put garlic in *everything*. Well, almost everything (my daughter once observed "there is no food that is not improved by adding either garlic or chocolate"). 

It tastes and smells fresh every time. Use about a teaspoon for each clove that the recipe calls for. Spending a half hour once a month for this streamlines cooking or assembling a dish. Note that after a few days it will tend to take on a bluish-green color, which is a bit disconcerting but doesn't affect the taste at all. If you've used too much vodka then over time the paste will settle and leave a layer of vodka at the top; you can pour this off if you like. I personally wouldn't drink it, but I suppose tastes vary.

One of my first culinary jobs was at a small brewery in Santa Cruz called Live Soup. They were famous for their garlic rosemary fries, but couldn't seemingly afford a food processor, so I would spend the first hour of my shift chopping garlic. I developed a fairly rapid technique for making minuscule diced garlic...

Unless your knife is stupid sharp, it won't cut you if it's just sliding Along the surface of your skin. So you can slide it between two fingers without cutting yourself. So I'd start with the garlic clove on its smaller flat side and hold it with two fingers on either side and run the knife between them to slice it into six or eight thin slices. Then roll it over onto its big flat side and repeat, holding everything in place, to make it into tiny juliennes. And finally rotate it ninety degrees and make it into tiny, uniform dice about 1mm square. I've tried to teach the method to several people but they've all been to afraid of cutting themselves to really learn it.

I would generally use a standard French style chefs knife, but as I have big hands, I've also done it with a cleaver like yours. It's a stretch, but I make it happen.
